Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation. These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.

title: Reconstruction-Augmented Visuomotor Pre-Training of 3D-Grounded Bimanual Dexterity from RGB-Only Human Videos
summary: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.

title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
comments: 103 pages (9 main), 15 figures, 68 tables. Project page: https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/ Code: https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.
comment: 103 pages (9 main), 15 figures, 68 tables. Project page: https://dolev31.github.io/lasagna/ Code: https://github.com/dolev31/lasagna

title: Sufficient and Necessary Causal Explanations for the Analysis of Autonomous Systems
summary: Understanding failures of autonomous systems is challenging, particularly when their behavior depends on black-box components such as neural networks. In this work, we make a distinction between two objectives of failure analysis: reproduction, which seeks to identify conditions sufficient to reproduce an observed failure, and avoidance, which seeks to identify the changes required to prevent it. Previous work on causal explanations of system failures is based on the concept of sufficient explanations and naturally supports reproduction. Nevertheless, we observe that it does not address the problem of avoiding the failure. In this paper, we introduce and formalize the concept of necessary explanations for system analysis as the correct formalism for failure avoidance. We place necessary explanations in the framework of actual causality and show that, together with sufficient explanations, they provide a unified causal framework for addressing both objectives of failure analysis. We present an efficient approximation algorithm for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal responsibility. We evaluate the efficiency of our approach across multiple environments. We demonstrate the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance through counterfactual generation and show that it outperforms existing methods.

title: Structure-Aware Message Passing on Petri Nets through Directed Walks and Incidence Diffusion
summary: A common application of the process mining discipline is to connect observed event data with Petri nets, which are bipartite, directed graphical process models with rich formal underpinnings. Recent work learns vector representations of Petri nets to retrieve process models and relate them to event logs, but leaves implicit two key aspects hidden within the net's structure: directed cycles (process loops) and invariants recorded by the net's incidence matrix. We expose both of these to message-passing graph neural networks, through a positional encoding built from return probabilities of directed place-transition walks (PNRWPE), and through same-type messages gated by diffusion kernels of the incidence matrix (DA-PNGNN). Our constructions raise macro balanced accuracy in predicting the generation factors of the 96 Process Discovery Contest 2023 models from 0.751 to 0.796 with PNRWPE, which nearly doubles accuracy on process loops, and to 0.830 with DA-PNGNN, which, without retuning, also improves net-to-tree retrieval top-1 accuracy on the self-supervised ProcRosetta benchmark by 4.1 to 5.9 points.

title: Accept or Repair: Preserving Passage-Supported Answers in Contrastive Decoding
comments: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code will be released at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/AoR
summary: Large language models often answer from knowledge learned during training, even when a provided passage contradicts that knowledge. To address this problem, contrastive decoding contrasts the predictions under the full and a modified prompt at every token, but it also alters correct answers that the passage supports. We show that checking answers against the passage removes this trade-off. Based on this observation, we propose Accept-or-Repair (AoR), a training-free procedure. AoR keeps a sampled answer if the passage supports it. Otherwise, it tries up to two replacements with contrastive decoding, returning one as soon as it passes this check. It rejects replacements that repeat the answer generated without the passage when the passage favors another answer. Our experiments show that AoR raises the score over sampling by 12.5 points on counterfactual passages and 2.3 on ordinary ones, surpassing eight contrastive and prompting baselines on both, including when each receives the same rejection rule. Replacing only initial answers that the passage does not support improves the average score of every decoder. These results suggest that models can follow passages that contradict their knowledge while preserving accuracy on passages that agree with it. Code will be released at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/AoR.
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code will be released at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/AoR

title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly. Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies. We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy. Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations. Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged. In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance. For SmolVLA, the head on the vision-language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs. We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings. Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs. With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement. These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.

title: Computing the Nucleon of Matching Games
summary: The nucleon is the multiplicative counterpart of the nucleolus: it lexicographically maximizes the fraction of its stand-alone value that each coalition receives. We study exact nucleon computation in matching games and in two extensions: $b$-matching games, in which players may have several partners, and partitioned matching games, in which one player may own several vertices. We resolve three open problems from a recent survey. For ordinary matching games with nonnegative rational weights, we give a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm using maximum-weight matching, shortest paths, and minimum-cost flow, ; it returns both a nucleon allocation and a compact description of the full nucleon. In contrast, computing any nucleon allocation is NP-hard for unit-weight $b$-matching games with capacities at most three and for unit-weight partitioned matching games of width at most three. Finally, for the unresolved capacity-two case, we show that exact nucleon computation is polynomial-time Turing reducible to SHORTEST NON-ZERO CYCLE.

title: SAKURA: Serving Attention Key-Value State Under Rate Adaptation for Private Image Editing on Phones
summary:
Diffusion transformers are widely used in image-editing services. To preserve both efficiency and privacy, existing systems commonly rely on cloud-device collaboration. Keeping request-specific inference on the device avoids sending personal images and prompts to the cloud. These workloads often use common templates, such as in face swapping and virtual try-on, enabling KV state to be precomputed and reused across requests. However, this reusable state is large and scales with the number of templates, making it impractical to store all of them on mobile devices. Storing them in the cloud addresses this capacity issue, but cache transfer is placed onto the inference path and can even be slower than on-device computation, especially under fluctuating mobile networks.
  We introduce SAKURA, a cloud-edge architecture that delivers reusable attention state to mobile devices under a bandwidth budget. It first uses a fine-grained token-importance-aware compression method to preserve image quality under limited transfer budgets. At runtime, SAKURA adaptively selects the cache representation for each upcoming shard based on network bandwidth. To enable efficient execution, we develop a pipelined runtime that overlaps cache transfer and reconstruction with on-device execution. We evaluate SAKURA using three editing tasks and two diffusion models, using a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone. SAKURA reduces latency by 1.82x and 3.27x over CacheGen adapted to DiT and on-device generation, respectively. It also reduces cache storage by 3.06x over uncompressed cache, while preserving image quality.

title: Monitorability Is Trainable: Post-Training for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
comments: The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model's reasoning is only useful to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.
comment: The first two authors contributed equally

title: Two Sides of the Same Proof: Extraction and Projection in Choreographic Programming
summary:
A new approach to the theory of choreographic languages has recently been proposed, based on the interpretation of choreographies with finite behaviors as proofs in an extension of linear logic.
  This paper further develops this approach to cyclic proofs to be capable of representing infinite behaviors, and prove a completeness result for choreographies with respect to the class of lock-free networks.
  We show that in a choreographies-as-proofs correspondence, the proof equivalence induced by rule permutations corresponds to bisimilarity, and that, under adequate assumption on the procedure definitions, the proof search procedure has a finite search space, and can be used to extract a choreography from a network.

title: Learning to Measure and Diagnose: A Clinical-Dictionary Radiomic Bottleneck Model for Thyroid Nodule Classification
summary: Thyroid ultrasound supports the assessment of nodule malignancy, but classification predictions often lack evidence linked to familiar clinical descriptions. Radiomics provides explicitly defined measurements that can support such explanations through a clinical dictionary. However, using these measurements as interpretable evidence requires reliable estimation from ultrasound images and preservation of measurement fidelity when optimizing classification performance. We propose a clinical-dictionary radiomic bottleneck model for thyroid nodule classification. Within this model, Family-Aware Radiomic Learning (FARL) estimates measurements with balanced supervision across feature families. Fidelity-Guided Bottleneck Modeling (FGBM) constructs a fixed bottleneck, followed by joint optimization of measurement estimation and classification under fidelity guidance. Decision evidence decomposition then traces feature contributions through a linear classifier and organizes them by clinical dictionary categories. Experiments on ThyroidXL and TN3K show competitive classification performance, while case studies illustrate feature contributions for benign and malignant nodules. These findings indicate interpretable classification with inspectable quantitative evidence informed by clinical knowledge. Code is available online.

title: APED-CXR: Adaptive Privileged Evidence Distillation for Chest X-Ray Grounding with Image-Only Inference
comments: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Compact chest X-ray (CXR) models that localize findings suit deployment, but box annotations are limited and report-aware multimodal models are expensive at inference. We introduce APED-CXR, which distills report-informed spatial evidence from a frozen multimodal teacher into a student with 11.1M parameters that predicts diseases and boxes from shared evidence maps and requires the image alone at test time. During training, the teacher uses the radiograph, report, and queried class to evaluate regions proposed from the student's current evidence maps, and its support scores serve as training targets for the student's pooled evidence scores within these regions. Trained on PadChest and evaluated on held-out PadChest-GR, refreshing the student's proposals for teacher evaluation improves box-level localization F1 from 0.302 with fixed warm-up proposals to 0.338 (IoU >= 0.5; gain 0.036, 95% CI [0.022, 0.049]), while maintaining diagnostic AUC. This gain depends on the teacher checking current proposals: with equally many random boxes, a fixed dense box set, teacher-generated boxes, or report rules instead of the teacher, F1 stays near the fixed-proposal level, and proposals two refreshes old recover only part of the gain. On NIH ChestX-ray14, a secondary test set, box recall also rises from 0.423 to 0.447.
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027

title: Engineering Requirements for Generative AI Agents: The BARD Process Theory
comments: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027)
summary: How teams engineer requirements for systems built around Generative AI (GenAI) Agents remains empirically uncharted. Existing Requirements Engineering (RE) research mainly addresses AI and ML-based systems broadly but provides no process account for agentic systems, whose non-deterministic behavior cannot be anticipated at design time. To understand how teams actually proceed, we applied Socio-Technical Grounded Theory across 36 semi-structured interviews with practitioners, interleaving data collection and analysis so that emerging findings drove our theoretical sampling and shaped successive rounds of coding. The result is Behavioral Agent Requirement Discovery (BARD), the process theory of RE for GenAI Agents. BARD holds that requirements are not fixed up front but discovered through a recurring cycle of four activities: teams scope the need, build the agent, observe its behavior, and revise what they ask for. Through this four-phase loop, the requirement evolves from a fixed specification towards behavioral and evaluation criteria. Four tensions drive transitions between phases, and two conditions frame the loop. BARD provides researchers with a framework for iteratively refining RE workflows, while giving practitioners a structured basis to embed into their development processes.
comment: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027)

title: On Almost MDS codes holding $(n-k-1)$-designs and an open problem on Witt design
summary: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an almost maximum distance separable (AMDS) code over the finite fields with parameters $[n,k,n-k]$ whose minimum-weight codewords support an $(n-k-1)$-$(n,n-k,λ)$ design. We first determine the parameters of the dual code $\mathcal{C}^{\bot}$. We also characterize the design and its complementary design supported by the minimum weight codewords of $\mathcal{C}^{\bot}$. In particular, we present explicit formulas for the weight enumerators of all subset codes of $\mathcal{C}^{\bot}$ with length at least $k+1$. These formulas are completely determined by the cardinality of the subset, the dimension, together with the parameter $λ$, and are independent of the specific choice of subsets. As an application, we answer an open problem posed by Wang, Tang and Ding in 2023 by proving that the $3$-design supported by the minimum-weight codewords in their proposed cyclic dual code is isomorphic to the complementary design of the Witt spherical geometry design.

title: LEAF-Mamba: Feature Adaptation and Fusion for Whole Slide Image Analysis
summary: Whole slide image (WSI) analysis enables computational diagnosis and prognosis, but gigapixel images and limited annotations make slide-level learning challenging. Multiple instance learning addresses this task by aggregating patch representations from frozen pretrained encoders. Recently, Mamba has enabled efficient modeling of long patch sequences. However, task supervision alone does not explicitly constrain information recovery during feature adaptation, while Mamba couples local processing with long-range propagation rather than retaining separate representations for fusion. Motivated by these challenges, we introduce LEAF-Mamba, a framework that jointly addresses latent evidence adaptation and fusion for frozen-feature WSI analysis. A reconstruction-regularized adapter learns compact, task-specific representations while reconstructing the input features. Parallel Mamba and convolutional streams then capture long-range dependencies and sequence-local interactions, with an input-dependent gate modulating their joint representation before slide-level pooling. Experiments across feature extractors demonstrate improved average performance over strong MIL baselines in both diagnostic classification and survival prediction. Component analyses further support the contributions of adaptation and fusion. These findings highlight the value of jointly designing feature transformation and contextual aggregation to translate pretrained representations into effective slide-level predictions.

title: Prompt Injection Through Forensic Evidence: A Taxonomy and Proof of Concept of Anti-Forensic Attacks on LLM-Assisted Digital Investigations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering digital forensics as examination assistants and autonomous agents. Digital forensics inverts the usual setting for indirect prompt injection: the evidence under analysis is attacker-controlled by definition, and the examiner is obliged to read it closely. This makes the reasoning layer a new anti-forensic target, next to the classical ones of data and tools. Classical anti-forensic taxonomies do not cover it, and prompt injection defences do not anticipate it. We extend the anti-forensic model to reflect the manipulation of reasoning, and present a taxonomy of attacks carried through adversarial evidence: an attacker selects an objective, a technique, a payload location, and a concealment method. We observe a perception gap, i.e., the fact that deterministic tools, the human examiner, and the model perceive the same evidence differently, which is what lets an injection reach the model unseen by the examiner. We demonstrate three attacks against an LLM-assisted analysis pipeline, changing a reported conclusion, writing attacker-chosen content to the analyst's workstation, and causing outbound network traffic, each driven only by text planted on the seized device. Mitigations to these attacks are also proposed.

title: Metamodel-Guided LLM Decoding for Consistent DSL Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software engineering artifacts written in domain-specific languages (DSLs). Correct DSL instances usually must comply with not only the concrete syntax but also the abstract syntax defined by a metamodel augmented with semantic well-formedness constraints. Existing constrained decoding approaches typically guarantee compliance only with concrete syntax or with a limited set of semantic constraints expressed over the generated text, making metamodel-level constraint consistency difficult to enforce during generation. We present MeMoDecode: a decoding framework that enforces a DSL's concrete syntax, abstract syntax, and well-formedness constraints jointly. Specifically, whenever the LLM generates a complete metamodel concept, MeMoDecode incrementally maps the current output to a partial model and verifies whether it can still be completed into a consistent instance. We combine MeMoDecode with a simple retry mechanism that resumes decoding from the most recent completable snapshot whenever an inconsistency is detected. Under a sound backend verifier, MeMoDecode never performs worse than grammar-constrained decoding on alignment metrics satisfying natural assumptions. Across four DSLs and six open-weight LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters, MeMoDecode achieves the highest consistency, improving consistency by 23% on average over unconstrained decoding and by 8% on average over grammar-constrained decoding. It also improves benchmark performance while incurring only modest runtime overhead. These results show that metamodel-guided decoding is an effective approach for enforcing DSL consistency during decoding across diverse DSLs and LLM scales.

title: Bridging Foundational and Agentic Capabilities of LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents, yet it remains unclear how their foundational capabilities translate into agentic capabilities. End-to-end scores leave unresolved whether low benchmark capability or weak deployment drives a failure, limiting actionable diagnosis. We bridge foundational and agentic capabilities through an operation-level measurement framework. We represent each model with a foundational profile derived from capability benchmarks and an operation profile derived from interaction trajectories, and define capability realization gaps as deviations of observed operation performance from predictions based on foundational capabilities. Experiments on fifteen model services in $τ^2$-Bench show that foundational profiles only partially predict agentic operations. Models with comparable profiles can differ substantially in execution, and these gaps remain consistent across task subsets. Operation profiles add information and substantially improve task-score prediction. The framework locates execution departures at the operation level to inform model development and agent evaluation. We will release our code and analysis artifacts.

title: VeruSteer: Learning What to Repair Next in Verus
summary: LLM-based verification systems repair Rust proofs by revising programs in response to Verus diagnostics. When several error types are reported, pipelines such as AutoVerus and VeruSAGE select the next repair target using a preset priority. Yet each repair changes the program and the errors that follow, so the same reported types can require different choices at different states. We present VeruSteer, which learns to select error types from the outcomes of alternative repair trajectories. It constructs repair trees offline and compares paths from the same initial program by verification success, repair rounds, and final verification progress. These comparisons supervise a selector that combines step-wise imitation with trajectory preference ranking. The selector uses self-attention over the program, verifier feedback, and earlier selections to rank the currently reported types. It replaces the default priority within a single repair trajectory, keeping the existing repair agents and adding no repair or verifier calls for selection. We evaluate VeruSteer by replaying its choices on stored AutoVerus and VeruSAGE test trees under four generation configurations. Across 1,270 test trees, VeruSteer increases verified outcomes from 185 to 194 (14.57\% to 15.28\%), gaining 12 successes and losing three for a net improvement of 0.71 percentage points. Among trees where the default fails but a recorded alternative verifies, VeruSteer succeeds on 3 of 4 AutoVerus trees and 9 of 11 VeruSAGE trees. Among trees with recorded alternatives where the default verifies, it retains success on 14 of 15 AutoVerus trees and 12 of 14 VeruSAGE trees. It also finds shorter successful trajectories and improves final progress on some trees where all recorded trajectories fail.

title: The Privacy Paradox Is a Misnomer: Data Under Structural Uncertainty
summary: The infamous privacy paradox refers to the apparent inconsistency between people's stated concern for privacy and their readiness to disclose personal information. This phenomenon has sparked two largely disconnected literatures: one offering experimental evidence of inconsistent behavior, and another providing qualitative accounts and defending the importance of privacy. The Article presents an online field experiment that bridges those literatures and shows that the so-called paradox arises from a mischaracterization of the underlying behavior. The Article finds that it is structural uncertainty about risk that drives seemingly paradoxical privacy decisions. It does so by isolating discounting mechanisms and empirically testing whether observed privacy choices reflect temptation or rational responses to uncertainty. The results suggest that privacy behavior is not paradoxical but, rather, consistent with choices shaped by incomplete information. The Article then discusses the policy implications of this reframing. As privacy decisions stem from structural uncertainty, which operates as a market failure, regulation should aim to reduce that uncertainty. This supports regulation that prioritizes transparency (for people to assess the risks of data collection) and flexibility mechanisms that accommodate evolving contexts. Such reframing provides a new argument for the right to be forgotten, which allows people to revisit prior disclosures as new risks become apparent. By shifting the focus from individual inconsistency to structural uncertainty, the findings call for privacy law to better reflect the reality of people's decision-making environments.

title: Information-Induced Conservatism Frontier of Distributed Stability Certificates
summary:
Conservatism in distributed stability certification is often treated as a limitation of the certificate itself, motivating richer Lyapunov functions, tighter relaxations, or stronger optimization. But a more fundamental limitation may arise from the reporting interface: once information is compressed, physically different systems can become indistinguishable. If stable and unstable systems produce the same report, no sound method can separate them. This paper asks where this information limit lies and how much additional information is needed to move it.
  We model information as an information structure that partitions admissible systems into information fibers. The strongest sound certificate for a fiber is determined by its smallest stability margin, yielding a method-independent benchmark. This separates total conservatism into information-induced and method-induced parts and characterizes information order, task sufficiency, and the stability value of additional information. Three network-node studies show that network-spectrum, scalar/eigenvalue-only passivity, and independent-local reports respectively lose network--node alignment, local directional alignment, and cross-node relation. They show that critical missing information is often relational rather than dimensional.
  We then move from diagnosis to information design. An information-conservatism frontier gives the smallest irreducible conservatism achievable under a prescribed budget, while its inverse gives the minimum information required for a target conservatism. A witness-pair characterization turns this into a weighted covering problem. Besides, a local sensitivity law provides a computable approximation and identifies valuable unresolved quantities. The framework indicates whether conservatism should be reduced by improving the certificate or enriching the information.

title: AssureCode: Structured Justification for Trustworthy Agentic Coding
summary: The use of AI-based tools in software development is rapidly changing how software is produced, enabling large volumes of code to be generated with limited human implementation effort. However, this raises fundamental challenges for ensuring that generated artifacts are aligned with developer intent and have been appropriately validated. In this work, we propose the use of structured argumentation in driving AI-assisted software development. Inspired by techniques from assurance engineering for safety-critical systems, we define a language of justification rationales that explicitly relate informal natural language prompts, formal specifications, assumptions about developer intentions, and program analysis evidence in a structured and verifiable format. We then describe AssureCode, a tool-supported methodology for creating such rationales as part of agentic code generation. We provide an empirical analysis of our implementation where we investigate its capacity to contribute towards justified assurance of correctness for AI-generated code.

title: OMAR: Open-World Multi-Attribute Reasoning for Scene-Conditioned Shelf Organization
summary: With the advent of foundation models, robots are increasingly capable of understanding and executing explicitly specified human tasks. Extending these capabilities to open-ended tasks, however, requires robots to infer appropriate actions from the observed scene. Household organization exemplifies this challenge, as robots must often act without detailed instructions, predefined object vocabularies, or known object-receptacle associations. While robots may follow instructions or learn organization preferences from demonstrations, inferring the latent organization of an occasionally changing scene and placing a novel object consistently with it remains challenging. We propose an open-world multi-attribute reasoning pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and constructs an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning. First, a vision-language model proposes labels together with attributes such as content and packaging type, which are grounded through segmentation, depth, and multi-view association. Then, an LLM reasons over this representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements without explicitly user-provided preferences. The resulting placement rankings guide subsequent geometric and kinematic feasibility checks for execution. Our experimental evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling autonomous placement of previously unseen objects without predefined object-receptacle mappings or class-specific retraining.

title: ALIAS: Evaluating Performance and Memorization in LLM-Written TLA+ Specifications
comments: 19 pages (8 main + appendix), 6 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/LUC-AI4FM/ALIAS
summary: Memorization inflates the benchmark scores of large language models (LLMs), since a model can reproduce answers it saw in training. Researchers test for it with consistent identifier renaming (CIR), which gives every identifier in a task a new name, and treat a lower score on the renamed task as evidence of recall. We test this method on the Temporal Logic of Actions Plus (TLA+) language, whose model checker acts as an oracle by confirming whether a renamed task preserves the exact behaviors of the original. Across 111 TLA+-Bench tasks, renaming lowers the correctness of Claude Opus 4.8 from 28% to 18% and of GPT-5 from 9% to 7%. Most of this decrease comes from how the test grades, which requires exact names that most descriptions never state. Grading by behavior shrinks the decrease to about 3 percentage points for Opus 4.8 and to 0 for GPT-5. In two model families fine-tuned on disjoint halves of the tasks, renaming removes about half of the training gain in likelihood and costs 4.9 percentage points (Qwen) and 1.3 percentage points (Gemma) on unseen tasks. A lower score after renaming therefore mixes memorization, name-based grading, and the cost of new names.
comment: 19 pages (8 main + appendix), 6 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/LUC-AI4FM/ALIAS

title: UniRAP: Towards Unified Part-level Physical Affordance Reasoning and Actionable Perception
summary: Vision-language perception has achieved impressive progress in aligning natural language with visual observations, yet grounding high-level semantics into part-level physical interaction remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose UniRAP, a unified model for inferring part-level physical affordances and mapping language instructions to actionable geometric representations. UniRAP formulates this problem as a conditional multimodal generation task, integrating visual inputs, textual instructions, and optional prompts into a shared spatiotemporal representation space through a unified interface token mechanism. To predict executable contact geometry, we introduce a Unified Affordance Decoder (UAD), which jointly performs object detection, part-level affordance segmentation, and 4-DoF interaction pose estimation by leveraging intermediate segmentation features. In addition, we propose a curriculum-based transfer training strategy that progressively adapts the model from general visual parsing to interaction-aware perception, improving data efficiency under limited textual annotations. Experiments show that UniRAP achieves state-of-the-art performance on referring expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction pose estimation, while maintaining strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic video scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of UniRAP as a unified perception framework for language-guided physical manipulation.

title: Location-of-interest vs. Current-location Privacy in Multi-hop Communication
summary: Consider a standard multi-hop wireless radio network in which nodes relay messages for one another. While the contents of messages may be sensitive and thus encrypted, the very fact that two radios communicated can leak sensitive information about both the physical location of the origin and the physical location of the destination. We investigate the trade-off between protecting the privacy of a user's current location and the privacy of their location of interest, and how the user should choose dummy destinations to obfuscate their queries.

title: Do Flow-Generation Tools Matter? Unsupervised Characterization of MQTT Traffic Across Public Datasets
summary:
Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT) is widely used in IoT environments due to its lightweight publish-subscribe design and suitability for resource-constrained networks. While current MQTT security studies mainly focus on detecting attacks and optimizing classification performance, this work takes a different perspective by presenting a cross-dataset, tool-aware characterization of MQTT traffic at the flow level. This perspective is motivated by the fact that flow-generation is tool-dependent: flows are not directly observed in packet captures, but are constructed through tool-specific decisions about packet grouping, flow termination, and feature export.
  Using packet captures from 4 public MQTT datasets, we generated over 380K flows with 3 open-access flow-generation tools: Zeek-flowmeter, Argus, and NTLFlowLyzer. We analyzed the tool-specific flows using K-means, DBSCAN, and HDBSCAN, with and without PCA-based dimensionality reduction. We measured clustering quality using 2 metrics: (1) Silhouette score to assess label-independent cluster compactness and separation, and (2) Adjusted Rand Index to measure agreement with available labels.
  Our results show that the choice of flow-generation tool affects the resulting flow population, feature-space structure, and clustering behavior. Zeek-flowmeter achieves the best performance in several settings, particularly with K-means and PCA reduction to 10 components. Yet, no single tool consistently dominates across all datasets, algorithms, and evaluation metrics. These findings show that flow-level MQTT analysis should treat the dataset, flow-generation tool, preprocessing choices, clustering algorithm, and evaluation metric as interconnected experimental factors.

title: Fully Dynamic Triangle and 4-Vertex Subgraph Counting: From Theory to Practice and Back Again
comments: Short version to appear at ALENEX 2027
summary:
Counting small patterns is a core primitive in large-scale graph analytics, with numerous applications in data management and network analysis. As modern graphs are massive and continuously evolving, maintaining such counts efficiently under updates is essential. Although specialized dynamic algorithms for patterns with up to four vertices exist, they remain largely theoretical; practitioners instead rely on general-purpose or approximate methods.
  We present an in-depth study of two dynamic approaches by Eppstein et al. and Hanauer et al. for maintaining counts of triangles and all connected four-vertex subgraph patterns, both based on variants of heavy-light vertex partitioning. We introduce theoretical and practical optimizations and develop hybrid variants that combine complementary strengths of both approaches.
  Experiments on 56 large real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs show that our optimized algorithms outperform the original methods and strong static and dynamic baselines on nearly all instances, both in total running time and worst-case update time, with speedups of up to several orders of magnitude. We further provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and tuning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive empirical study of heavy-light partitioning for dynamic subgraph counting, and our findings may inform other algorithms based on this technique.
comment: Short version to appear at ALENEX 2027

title: Key Findings for Small UAS for Post-Disaster Damage Assessment from the CURSE'26 Exercise
summary: The CLARKE building and road damage assessment AI classifier was incorporated into the Catastrophic Unmanned Remote Sensing Exercise (CURSE) 2026, which trained 23 small uncrewed aerial systems (sUAS) teams from state and local agencies and non-governmental organizations in Florida and Missouri on how to collect imagery for an incident command Remote Sensing Cell. Although CLARKE has been operationally deployed to two hurricanes (Debby and Helene), CURSE'26 presented an opportunity to evaluate the machine learning model with a larger set of never-before-seen orthomosaics. The results show that building and road damage assessment together ran in 3.5 minutes on average, and that building damage assessment achieved a Micro F1 of 0.834 with no manual adjustments to correct spatial misalignment and delivered that performance in both Florida and Missouri, demonstrating good geographic transfer. It also showed that road damage assessment performed poorly due to sensitivity to misalignment between road maps and the images, and to lighting and environmental conditions in an urban setting. The analysis of CURSE'26 presents five other findings of value to the sUAS community: that the use of sUAS and machine learning is now operationally normalized and accepted, sUAS teams in the field can improve classification accuracy by timing their flights, exercises are good operational tests but their value for evaluating learning models is less clear, edge computing is needed to overcome the wireless upload barrier, and the application of sUAS and AI to disaster response has ethical and legal ramifications for pilots and data managers.

title: JointLight: Human-Centric Video Relighting with Asynchronous RGB-Irradiance Joint Modeling
summary: Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real- world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. The code and dataset will be publicly released.

title: An experimental evaluation of static k-center clustering algorithms on graphs
summary: The $k$-center problem is one of the most fundamental clustering problems and has applications in a wide range of areas, including facility location, network design, data mining, and machine learning. Given a set of objects together with a distance measure, the goal is to select $k$ centers such that the maximum distance from any object to its closest center is minimized. The $k$-center problem has been studied extensively from a theoretical perspective, both in metric spaces and on graphs. While there have been experimental studies for $k$-center clustering in metric spaces, a comprehensive experimental comparison of graph-based $k$-center algorithms on large-scale graphs is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge this gap by evaluating a set of algorithms ranging from classical approaches such as Gonzalez's greedy algorithm [TCS 1985], an algorithm based on the framework established by Hochbaum and Shmoys [Math. Oper. Res. 1985], to more recent methods, including algorithms by Thorup [SICOMP 2001] and Abboud et al. [SOSA 2023]. Our study considers both running time, solution quality and the effects of parallelism on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art $k$-center algorithms on graphs and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches in practice.

title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
summary: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.

title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI?
comments: 18 pages, 4 figures. Companion paper to arXiv:2601.13749
summary: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Companion paper to arXiv:2601.13749

title: D-Pingmesh: Dynamic Probing and Fault Localization for Reconfigurable Datacenter Networks
comments: 15 pages, 13 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (SIGOPS ATC 2026)
summary: Pingmesh monitors datacenter networks through periodic pings between servers. In reconfigurable datacenter networks, topology engineering (TPE) and traffic engineering (TE) make uniform server-pair probing inefficient: a pinglist wastes budget retesting common paths while missing low-probability interfaces. Frequent control-plane updates further require rapid pinglist refresh, and cause path ambiguity at control-plane boundaries for fault localization. We present D-Pingmesh, a probing and fault-localization system co-designed with the TPE/TE control plane. Its control-plane-aware generator builds task-efficient pinglists by greedily admitting probes with high interface coverage under the current TPE/TE snapshot. An incremental replay-and-repair mechanism updates pinglists across reconfigurations rather than recomputing from scratch. At control-plane boundaries, a Rho-EM localizer jointly infers per-task old/new-path mixture weights and the fault set through EM-style iteration. We evaluate D-Pingmesh on an 8-pod reconfigurable topology under dynamic TPE/TE. At a 0.99 coverage target, D-Pingmesh uses 17.7x fewer tasks than Pingmesh and generates each pinglist about 5.1x faster than RD-Probe. In ns-3 simulation, boundary-aware localization improves micro F1 from 0.871 to 0.953 over the deTector PLL baseline. A testbed deployment demonstrates second-scale fault localization with low host overhead. These results demonstrate that D-Pingmesh is practical for reconfigurable datacenter networks with control-plane-aware monitoring.
comment: 15 pages, 13 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (SIGOPS ATC 2026)

title: Open-Vocabulary Models and Label Propagation for Uncertainty-aware Pseudo-Labeling of Object Detection Datasets
summary: Object detection models rely on large-scale annotated datasets that require substantial manual annotation effort. The labeling costs further increase when annotation uncertainty is captured through soft labels, as multiple annotations must be collected for each object. We address this challenge by introducing a semi-supervised framework for the uncertainty-aware annotation of object detection datasets. Our approach leverages open-vocabulary object detectors to generate region proposals and semantically meaningful object representations. Based on these representations, we construct an object-level similarity graph and propagate probabilistic label information. Our framework assigns soft labels to previously unlabeled objects, quantifying both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. We evaluate our method on four object detection benchmarks with soft-label annotations and demonstrate that high-quality annotations can be obtained with only a small fraction of manually labeled objects. Furthermore, we show that detectors trained on semi-automatically annotated data achieve performance comparable to models trained on fully manually annotated data. We achieve state-of-the-art downstream detection performance for the task of semi-supervised object detection on the COCO dataset, with 40.5% AP virtually matching the performance of the model trained on fully manually constructed data (40.9%) at only 1% of labeling costs. These results highlight the potential of open-vocabulary models and graph-based label propagation for efficient, accurate and uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling.

title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum-based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query-intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub-query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub-queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

title: Stability analysis of boundary element methods for the wave equation: The weakly singular operator in $1d$
summary: We discuss the construction of stable discrete pairs of trial and test spaces for the wave equation. Building on a general abstract operator-theoretic framework, we show how optimal pairings can be derived for a one-dimensional boundary element formulation of the wave equation with prescribed Dirichlet data, based on an indirect single layer potential ansatz. In this setting, the optimal test space can be computed analytically and has a physical interpretation, reflecting the non-local nature of the underlying operator.

title: Asymmetric Likelihood-Free Hypothesis Testing
summary:
In likelihood-free hypothesis testing (LFHT), given samples from two unknown distributions $P,Q$ on $[n]$ with $\mathrm{d_{TV}}(P,Q)\geq\varepsilon$, and from a third distribution $D\in\{P,Q\}$, the goal is to identify whether $D=P$ or $D=Q$. We study asymmetric likelihood-free hypothesis testing, where the sample budgets $s_P$ and $s_Q$ for $P$ and $Q$ may differ, and characterize the feasible triples $(s_P,s_Q,s_D)$ up to logarithmic factors. We establish that unequal reference budgets can give a polynomial saving. For instance, for constant separation, $n$ samples from $P$ and $n^{3/4}$ from $Q$ allow testing with $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ samples from $D$, whereas both existing baselines---symmetric LFHT and unequal-sample closeness testing---require $Ω(\sqrt n)$ samples from $D$.
  We further apply our results to non-adaptive distribution 2-clustering, where the sample allocation among $k$ distributions must be fixed before observing any data. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds for this problem up to logarithmic factors in terms of the domain size, number of distributions, smaller cluster size, and separation, both with one cluster distribution known and with both unknown. Comparing with known bounds for adaptive sample allocation gives a worst-case adaptivity gap of $\widetildeΘ(k^{1/4})$.

title: Prefix Visibility Ratio: Quantifying Partial Observability in Carpet Bombing Detection
summary: Carpet bombing attacks distribute malicious traffic across many destinations within a network prefix, while operational monitoring commonly provides destination-specific telemetry for only a subset of those targets. This creates an attack-conditional observability problem that is not captured by address utilization or nominal monitoring coverage. We introduce the Prefix Visibility Ratio (PVR), defined as the fraction of attacked destinations for which the telemetry required by the host-level evidence plane is available, and argue that PVR should be treated as an explicit evaluation dimension for carpet bombing detection. We then present VANTA (Visibility-Aware Network Threat Analysis) as one concrete way to operationalize this principle. VANTA combines host-level and prefix-level anomaly scores, estimates PVR online from router-side destination evidence and the monitored-destination inventory, and adjusts evidence fusion according to both estimated visibility and estimator confidence. Across a validated campaign of 2,160 Mininet runs, VANTA achieves 99.18% precision, 93.46% recall, a global F1-score of 96.24%, and a 1.54% false-positive rate. In a separate matched-observability study using task-adapted feature-level reference implementations, VANTA reaches 95.89% pooled F1 and 92.39% recall for configured PVR<=10%, with its largest advantage appearing at configured PVR=1%. These reference comparisons are intended to isolate observability effects under a common binary detection task rather than to reproduce the original end-to-end objectives of the referenced systems. The results establish attacked-destination visibility as a measurable factor that can materially change detector behavior and should be reported explicitly in future carpet bombing evaluations.

title: In vitro starch digestion kinetic, formal analysis and new kinetic model
summary: Describing mathematically the kinetics of the enzymatic hydrolysis of starch is a crucial part of nutrition and industrial applications studies. The majority of math models aim to fit the hydrolysis-extent curve ($X\_t$), so-called digestogram, whose simple shape which can be fitted equally well by various math models. A relevant model of starch digestion kinetics should be more specific of the phenomenon. This study proposes a novel analytical framework that jointly fits the hydrolysis-extent curve ($X\_t$) and the instantaneous reaction-rate coefficient ($k\_a(t)$). A large dataset comprising 672 wheat-starch time-course measurements (including normal, waxy, and high-amylose genotypes), and additional experiments on other botanical starches was analysed. Standard First-Order and Weibull models were compared with two newly derived kinetic formulations \eqref{Eq.11} and \eqref{Eq.12} based on expected starch hydrolysis' phenomenon by which $k\_a(t)$ tends with time towards an asymptotic-rate constant value, $k\_e$, following a characteristic relaxation time ($τ$). A mathematical proof of the existence of $k\_e$, specific of the type of starch, is provided, based on an analysis of the Weibull's parameters. Model ability to fit both $X\_t$ and $k\_a(t)$ was assessed by examining coefficients of determination ($R^2$) for both data types, and its adjusted version ($R^2\_{adj}$) was used to compare performances between models. All models fit very well $X\_t$ data, while $k\_a(t)$ is much more discriminant of the model formulation. Wheat starch types are well distinguished, regarding ke, by the new models, with higher susceptibility to amylase for waxy samples ($\approx 5.7\times 10^{-3} min^{-1}$), than normal ($\approx 2.2\times 10^{-3} min^{-1}$) and high-amylose ($\approx 1.7\times 10^{-3} min^{-1}$) ones. The new models outperformed the other models for monotonic evolution of $k\_a(t)$, particularly digestion of high-amylose, and allow a more accurate estimation of $k\_e$. However, the analysis also highlighted limitations for modelling non-monotonic kinetics observed for waxy wheat starch digestion, suggesting a need for more sophisticated differential-equation descriptions for $k\_a(t)$. Overall, the combined fitting strategy provides a robust method for extracting physically meaningful kinetic parameters, facilitating deeper insight into the factors controlling starch digestion and supporting the development of more accurate predictive models for glycaemic response and food processing.

title: Some Results on the Weight Spectrum of Binary Reed-Muller Codes $RM(m-7,m)$
summary: We study the set of weights occurring in the high-order binary Reed-Muller codes $RM(m-7,m)$. For every $m\geq 14$, we prove that the weight spectrum contains all even weights in $[336,2^m-336]$, together with an explicit finite set of low weights and their complements. The proof first establishes the corresponding base-code inclusion in $RM(7,14)$. This base step uses four-block concatenation, explicit degree-six monomial witnesses, and known spectrum inputs for $RM(5,10)$ and $RM(6,12)$. The base inclusion is then lifted to all $m\geq 14$ by a concatenation-based induction. We also analyze the remaining base-code target weights $322,326,330,334$ in several restricted families, including four-block branches, affine-flat and structured inner corrections in a fixed Carlet-type Maiorana-McFarland outer shell, and sparse sums of degree-7 coordinate monomials. The residual analysis delineates several construction routes that cannot yield the four unresolved base-code weights, thereby sharpening the remaining $c=7$ spectrum problem.

title: On the maximum length of cyclic MDS codes
summary: We study the maximum length of nontrivial simple-root cyclic maximum distance separable (MDS) codes over ${\mathbb F}_q$. We prove $n\le q+1$ if $\gcd(n,q^2-1)>2$, or if the dimension is even and $\gcd(n,q^2-1)>1$. The bound also holds for all lengths whose prime factors lie in $\{2,3,5,7\}$. We obtain further cases involving primes $\ell\ge11$ with $(\ell-1)/2$ prime, under conditions on the exponents and the characteristic. The proofs combine Fourier supports, locality bounds and field descent with arithmetic restrictions on multiplicative orders and prime-adic valuations.

title: Compositionality with Primitives: A Unified View from Euclidean to Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
comments: Accepted at WACV 2027 Main Conference, 17 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables
summary: Compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel combinations of previously observed objects and attributes. Prior work showed that large-scale vision-language models encode decomposable semantic structures that can be recomposed to enable generalization. The Geodesically Decomposable Embeddings (GDE) framework formalizes this by identifying directions in the tangent space at the Frechet mean of the embedding distribution, which encode primitive visual concepts. Unseen attribute-object compositions can be synthesized through vector addition of these primitives. We revisit the assumption that compositional generalization requires explicit attribute-object pair re-composition. By means of new compositional scoring functions and extensive evaluations, we show that directly using the decomposed primitives suffices for recognizing unseen compositions. In that, we gain insights on how the geometry of the embedding manifold (Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic) and dataset structure affect compositional reasoning. Across models (CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, HyCoCLIP), we show that compositional structure consistently emerges as primitive representations, enabling inference on CZSL benchmarks (MIT-States, VAW-CZSL, UT-Zappos50K, Clothing16K) and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA. Code: https://github.com/nis-research/Compositionality-with-Primitives.
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027 Main Conference, 17 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables

title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
comments: Accepted to the Agentic AI for Biological Discovery (AgenticLS) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.
comment: Accepted to the Agentic AI for Biological Discovery (AgenticLS) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: COMET: A coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems
comments: for associated GitHub repository, see https://github.com/nicmig/COMET
summary: Incorporating AI systems into safety systems requires monitoring to avoid silent faults and ensure safe and reliable operation. Single monitors often do not provide actionable information for human supervisors, who act as the system's adaptive controller. We present COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems in which each monitor is anchored in a different fault mode. Monitor outputs are combined in a coordination layer and mapped by a communication layer to a traffic-light display. In this work, COMET consists of three monitoring layers: signal integrity, physics consistency, and the AI system's competence envelope. The framework is evaluated on an open dataset of compressed-air leaks, where an AI system detects leaks from acoustic emissions, with held-out conditions simulating covariate shift, semantic shift, and sensor faults, events expected during runtime but unknown in their exact appearance. All monitors are frozen after development and tested zero-shot, and the framework is compared against no-monitoring and single-monitor setups. The bare AI system fails silently and confidently under all three shift types, whereas COMET reduces the trusted-wrong-answer rate to zero on covariate-shifted no-leak data and on three of four sensor faults, at a nominal false-alarm rate of $\approx 1\%$. Single monitors come close in detection but cannot attribute the fault mode. COMET converts their anonymous detection flags into diagnoses. Residual silent misses under semantic shift define the boundary of passive monitoring. Runtime monitoring frameworks for AI-enabled safety systems must therefore combine quantitative fault detection and isolation with qualitative, human-oriented feedback.
comment: for associated GitHub repository, see https://github.com/nicmig/COMET

title: Pfaffian Recognition is in coRP
summary: A graph is called Pfaffian if it admits a Pfaffian orientation. The Pfaffian recognition problem asks whether a given graph is Pfaffian. In 1989, Vazirani and Yannakakis showed that this problem is polynomial time equivalent to testing whether a prescribed orientation is Pfaffian, and that the problem belongs to $\mathsf{coNP}$. The complexity of the problem for general graphs has remained open since then. For bipartite graphs, polynomial time recognition algorithms were obtained by Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas in 1999, and independently by McCuaig in 2004. We show that testing whether a given orientation is Pfaffian can be reduced to polynomial identity testing. This gives a randomized polynomial time algorithm for Pfaffian recognition on general graphs, placing the problem in $\mathsf{coRP}$.

title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
summary: Long contexts increase the memory cost of the key-value (KV) cache in large language model (LLM) inference. Sparse attention reduces attention computation and memory traffic by selecting historical tokens, but the retained KV cache must remain available for later decoding steps. We present UlaCache, a KV cache management system built around a unified logical address space spanning GPU KV pools and optional CPU memory. Stable logical references let the inference engine allocate and select KV independently of physical placement. Common allocation and sparse-access interfaces support data-parallel (DP) and tensor-parallel (TP) attention. For distributed storage, local GPU buffers retain selected KV across decoding steps, so only missing entries require transfers. When CPU storage is enabled, Parallel Bucketed LRU (PB-LRU) manages a GPU pool shared across requests. It updates recency metadata and selects eviction victims in parallel. UlaCache transfers KV and then updates the address mappings. With speculative decoding enabled under matched CPU and GPU memory budgets, UlaCache achieves peak decoding throughput speedups of 1.16 $\times$ (DP) and 1.70 $\times$ (TP) on H200, and 1.73 $\times$ (DP) and 2.51 $\times$ (TP) on B300, compared with the state-of-the-art baseline.

title: Controlling Variability in~Neuroimaging Analysis Pipelines with~Software Product Lines
summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an acquisition technique used for medical diagnosis. It is notably used for structural and functional MRI (or fMRI) image analysis. MRI data is known to be complex and noisy, so pipelines are created to extract and enhance relevant information in retrieved images. The NARPS study highlighted the significant variability that can emerge from different pipelines set up by independent teams while trying to answer the same research question about brain functioning. Having different implementations realizing the same task is a typical playground for software product lines (SPLs), which may be out of the sight of neuroimage practitioners. Thus, proposing an SPL out of these different pipelines falls back on a typical reverse-engineering problem with its usual difficulties. In this document, we advocate for the conceptual adoption of SPL principles as a promising direction to improve reproducibility and consistency in neuroimaging research.

title: UserSWE: Evaluating Coding Agents in Multi-Turn Conversations with Dynamic Users
summary: As coding agents become more capable, developers increasingly use them to fix bugs through multi-turn interactions. Existing benchmarks do not adequately cover this scenario. Most present a complete issue report in a single turn without interaction. Their evaluation can produce both false positives and false negatives, accepting incorrect patches or rejecting correct ones. We introduce UserSWE for evaluating coding agents' ability to fix repository-level bugs through multi-turn interactions with dynamic users and execution-grounded verdicts at every turn. Its construction pipeline turns repository history and existing single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn tasks. At each turn, information pools constrain what the simulated user can reveal, while a persona chain sampled from a transition model calibrated on 20,859 development sessions governs how it speaks. Tests run after every turn, and a pair of agents from different model families writes and gates each verdict, using test results as primary evidence and model judgment only for aspects the tests cannot resolve. We evaluate eleven agents on 72 tasks from 42 repositories and find that agent rankings change with the interaction budget. Claude Fable 5.1 resolves the most tasks in one turn, GPT-6-Astra resolves the most by the eighth turn, and Claude Opus 5 leads at most intermediate budgets. These results indicate that single-turn performance is insufficient to characterize interactive coding ability.

title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
summary: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. On one LoCoMo conversation (419 turns, 152 questions), we run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code), each with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5, and record what every rollout costs. This is a short empirical study, with one conversation and one run per cell. Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out. With Claude Opus 5.5, Pi tops the cost-accuracy frontier, scoring 99% for less than half the cost of full context; its one miss is a wrong answer key. Part of that lead comes from photo captions that only the agents could read: on the 88 questions whose evidence has no photo, Pi and full context differ by one answer.

title: GuidedSAM-Plume: An Expert-Guided Segmentation Framework for Volcanic Plumes
summary: Quantitative analysis of environmental phenomena increasingly relies on image-based measurements. In volcanology, the geometric characterization of volcanic plumes and clouds from RGB images remains hindered by the scarcity of dedicated segmentation solutions and partially handcrafted annotations remain widely prevalent. We present GuidedSAM-Plume, an open-source expert-guided framework tailored for the interactive segmentation of volcanic plumes and clouds. It leverages the zero-shot, spatial prompt-based capabilities of SAM2. The framework was thoroughly validated on a challenging dataset through dedicated segmentation metrics and field-relevant volcanological descriptors. From minimal user inputs, it is able to significantly increase performance compared to fully automatic dedicated solutions while preserving the reliability of derived volcanological parameters. The absence of retraining requirements lowers adoption barriers within the volcanological community, and the framework's demonstrated suitability for complex, diffuse plume-shaped phenomena extends its applicability to broader environmental science domains. The re-annotated dataset, produced under the guidance of expert volcanologists within the proposed framework, ultimately yields a more standardized release. The framework and accompanying dataset are made available at https://github.com/tad-damo/GuidedSAM-Plume.

title: Early versus Late RGB-Infrared Fusion for Counter-UAV Detection: A Comparative Study
